name: Python
title: Python (2.7)
lifecycleNote: The Python 2 series ended on 2020-04-20 with 2.7.18; no further release or security fix is planned.

preamble.text: Analysis against Python 2.7 (released 2010-07-03, final release 2.7.18 on 2020-04-20): `print` is a statement, `str` is bytes, `async` does not exist, and `dict` iteration order is unspecified. The family's Python 3.14 page assesses the current release.

type.text: **Dynamic typing**: the type of a value is whatever the run time finds, so every agreement is deferred to execution
**The call target is chosen from the value**: a method name must exist on every object that arrives at the site
**No sum type**: an alternative is a sentinel, a `None`, or a tuple with a tag, and exhaustiveness stays a convention
**No type parameter**: an algorithm over several types duplicates or falls back on one universal object
**`None` is an ordinary value**: no signature says a value may be absent, and each consumer writes the guard
**A signature states no effects**: a call may read a file, mutate a module global, and raise, and the signature names only the return value
**`ctypes` is an unchecked boundary**: a hand-written declaration states the C layout, and nothing validates it

construction.text: **A module-level name is a global**: a function writes the caller's namespace through `global`, and any module can reach the name
**Bindings are mutable by default**: nothing states that a name or an attribute will not change
**Dictionary order is the hash's**: the 2.7 reference states that the order of `dict` keys is unspecified, and insertion order becomes a promise only in 3.7
**`__init__` may run side effects**: construction and initialisation are one call, and a subclass shares the base's path
**One value, many names**: names bind objects, and a parameter, a closure, and an attribute can hold the same list
The import system executes a module once, at first import; a circular import hands the importer the half-initialized module

memory.text: **Reference counting reclaims at the last reference**: most objects are released as soon as nothing names them
**A cycle needs the collector**: a reference loop waits for the periodic pass
**`__del__` timing is not a release path**: a finalizer is unreliable for a resource
**No release runs at scope exit**: `with` releases only the context managers that exist, and a lock or a file acquired outside one has no scope rule
**A module global extends a lifetime**: a name held at module level keeps its object alive for the process
**No handle names its owner**: any two names reach the same mutable object

error.text: **`try`/`except` carries a failure to the frame that handles it**: a raise is a value that unwinds
**A failure may arrive undeclared**: a raised exception needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it
**A bare `except` catches everything**: the declaration is the handler's choice, not the raiser's
**A failure is not a value**: a `raise` cannot be folded into an expression, so each level rebuilds the `try`/`except` shape around the call

concurrency.text: **The interpreter lock serialises bytecode**: a CPU-bound program must leave the language, through a process or a native extension, to use a second core
**Shared state is the default**: a global or an attribute is reachable from every thread
**Nothing detects a race**: the lock discipline is an agreement across modules
**No scope joins a thread**: `threading.Thread` is started and joined by hand, so a task can outlive the code that started it

platform.text: **No company owns the language**: Python is governed by the Python Software Foundation
**Several implementations exist**: CPython, PyPy, Jython, and IronPython are separate runtimes
**The runtime is portable**: CPython builds on the era's operating systems and on many others
**The packaging tools are vendor-neutral**: the package index and the installer are not tied to one vendor

performance.text: **Interpreted**: the bytecode dispatch, not the algorithm, decides the shape of a hot loop
**A C extension helps and binds the program to the C ecosystem**: the fast path is a native module
**Object overhead is high**: an integer and a list are heap objects

ecosystem.text: **The package index holds the ecosystem**: a dependency is fetched by the installer
**The tooling is settled**: pip, virtualenv, and setuptools cover the workflow
**A wheel binds to an interpreter**: the filename names the Python, ABI, and platform tags, and the installer loads that binary [@pep425; @pep384]
**Stored byte-code binds to the release**: the marshal format carries a magic number per release and no cross-release promise [@pyPickle]

evolution.text: **The Python 3 split**: `print` becomes a function, `str` becomes text, division changes meaning, and the standard library is reorganised, so a 2.7 codebase is revisited across the boundary
**No steward for the line**: the series is retired, so a defect in 2.7 is permanent and the only migration path lies outside it
**A bug-fix-only line**: 2.7 added no new syntax after 2.7.0, so the definition of the line is stable

domain.text: **Data analysis is the language's main work**: NumPy, SciPy, and pandas run on 2.7
**Scripting and automation**: a short program drives an operating system or another program
**A web back end is built from it**: Django and its peers run on the release

learning.text: **A gentle start**: the syntax reads as executable pseudocode
**A large literature**: tutorials and courses exist for every level

syntax.text: **Indentation carries the block**: the structure is the layout
**Indentation is also the failure**: a mixed tab and space is a syntax error the reader cannot see

testing.text: **`unittest` ships with the runtime, and pytest is a standard dependency**: a runner and an assertion library are available
**`pdb` ships with the runtime**: the toolchain steps through the source
**A mistake is found on the path that runs**: the compiler decides nothing, so coverage is the only evidence of safety
**The only published clock is the wall**: `time.time` reads the operator's calendar, and `time.clock` reports processor time rather than elapsed time

security.text: **No pointer is available**: a buffer overflow and a use-after-free are not expressible
**A value from outside arrives with no declared type**: keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer's check
**`eval` and `exec` turn text into code**: a data path can become a control path

reproducibility.text: **Builds are not byte-reproducible by default**: archive metadata and build paths reach the artifact
**Dependencies resolve without a lock**: an unpinned requirement is resolved from the index at install time
**The interpreter is not pinned by the project**: the release is left to a virtual environment or an image

supplychain.text: **The index publishes signed metadata**: the installer verifies a package's origin
**The index is a flat name space**: a name is a first claim, and a dependency can be redirected without a change in the consumer's source
**A vulnerability feed joins advisories to package versions**: OSV covers this registry

observability.text: **The instrumentation standard publishes an implementation**: traces and metrics have a stable expressed form

feedback.text: **The edit is the run**: no build step sits between a change and its effect

interop.text: **A general foreign-function interface exists**: `ctypes` and the C extension API reach native code in process

governance.text: **The specification is public**: the language reference states the language, and the enhancement proposals record the changes
**A published parser exists**: the runtime ships `ast`, and its grammar source is public

tradeoffs: **Readable syntax vs. hidden rules**: the indentation that makes the code readable is also the rule a mixed file breaks silently
**A batteries-included library vs. an audit surface**: the standard library is large and stable, so a reviewer decides which of its modules are still the right place for a job
**Comprehensions vs. the loop**: an expression that builds a list hides the accumulation in one line, and a reader who needs the loop's control flow rewrites it
verdict: Python 2.7 is the last release of the Python 2 line and the clearest example of a language that outgrew its own dialect. It is dynamic, garbage-collected, module-scoped, and readable, and it carries no type system, no effect tracking, and no sum type. Its costs are the costs of its era: `print` is a statement, `str` is bytes, a dictionary has no promised order, the only clock is the wall, and no scope runs a release. The interpreter lock forbids parallel bytecode, and the line itself ended in 2020, so a defect in 2.7 is permanent. Main strength: the era's most productive language for data work and glue code. Main weakness: the 2.x line is a dead end by construction, and the move to 3.0 revisits every file. The family's Python 3.14 page assesses the successor.

energy.text: Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path is published for the language itself; a safety-critical deployment rests on a platform vendor's qualified runtime, not on the language.

delivery.note: A source distribution builds on the target machine
The wheel filename names the interpreter, ABI, and platform tags, and pip installs that binary

data_formats.note: Python publishes the promise for pickled data: the format is guaranteed backwards compatible across Python releases provided a compatible pickle protocol is chosen, and each protocol version is named for the release that first reads it
Python states that the marshal serialization format is not guaranteed to be portable across Python versions, and that the implementers reserve the right to change it in non-backwards compatible ways
